Need to check the proof carefully, especially the Lemma's induction and step (1), and the final counting.

Check (1): unboundedness fine. m not a term, m≥A... wait if m = A, it's a term. If m > A, not a term, then since sequence unbounded there is n with a_n < m (m > A = a_1). Need m < a_{n+1}: pick n largest with a_n < m; since unbounded, a_{n+1} > m. If m shared factor with all a_1..a_n, then a_{n+1} ≤ m, contradiction. So m is coprime to some a_i (i ≤ n). Good. Actually also need m ≥ A so that m ≥ a_1, fine; if m > A it's after first term. Fine.

Lemma induction: induction over sequence terms in increasing order. σ(x) nonempty: x = A clear; later term shares prime with A, that prime ≤ A? A prime dividing A is ≤ A, yes. Wait σ(x) = P(x)∩Q where Q = primes ≤ A. Common prime with A divides A, so ≤ A. Good.

Case all prime factors ≤ A: σ(x)=P(x) good by (1) — but wait (1) requires x ≥ A; x is a term so x ≥ A. Good.

Otherwise pick prime q > A dividing x. R = product of primes in σ(x) (nonempty). Choose p ∈ σ(x), k ≥ 0 least with m = R p^k ≥ A. P(m) = σ(x)? m = R p^k has prime support σ(x) ∪ {p} = σ(x). Yes.

m < x: if k=0, m=R < Rq ≤ x since q | x and R | x? Is R | x? R = product of primes in σ(x) each to first power — divides x since each prime in σ(x) divides x. Yes R | x, and Rq | x, Rq ≤ x, R < Rq. Good. If k>0: R p^{k-1} < A, so p^k < pA/R ≤ A (since p ≤ A... p ∈ Q so p ≤ A, R ≥ p? R contains p so R ≥ p, hence pA/R ≤ A). So m = R p^k < R·A ≤ Rq? Need R p^k < Rq: p^k < A < q. Yes. Good.

If m = A: then σ(x) = P(A)... fine, σ(x) good since P(A) is good (contains P(A) good? P(A) itself: A is a term so P(A) good). Actually they say m is first term. OK.

Else m > A. Suppose m not a term. "The proof of (1) applied causally" gives sequence term b < m coprime to m. Hmm, (1)'s proof: m > A, m not a term ⇒ exists a_i coprime to m, and a_i < m? The argument: choose n with a_n < m < a_{n+1}; then m coprime to some a_i, i ≤ n, so a_i < m. Yes b < m.

But b < m < x, so b is a sequence term smaller than x — is b necessarily a term at an earlier position in the sequence? Sequence is increasing, terms in increasing order = index order. Yes b = a_i with i < index of x? b < x and both terms, so index of b < index of x. Induction hypothesis: σ(b) good. Then σ(b) ∩ P(x) ≠ ∅: σ(b) good means it meets P(a_i) for every i. Does it meet P(x)? Goodness: σ(b) meets every P(a_i) including... wait goodness defined as meeting P(a_i) for all i. Since x is a term a_j, σ(b) meets P(x). Yes (2).

gcd(b,m)=1, P(m)=σ(x), so σ(b) ∩ σ(x) = ∅. Primes of σ(b) all ≤ A; primes of P(x)\σ(x) all > A. So σ(b) ∩ P(x) = ∅. Contradiction. So m is a term. Then P(m)=σ(x) good by (1). Induction complete. Solid.

Wait — one subtlety: induction is over all terms x = a_j; but the induction hypothesis is used only for b which is a term with b < x — need b's index < j: yes since sequence strictly increasing.

(3): m term ⇔ P(m) good (1); forward: lemma gives σ(m) good. Reverse: σ(m) ⊆ P(m), upward closed — need "goodness upward closed": if S good and S ⊆ S', then S' meets every P(a_i) too. Yes. So σ(m) good ⇒ P(m) good ⇒ m term. Good.

(4): σ(m+L) = σ(m) for p ∈ Q: p | L so p|m+L ⇔ p|m. But m+L could have large prime factors — irrelevant, σ only. Also need σ(m) nonempty for equivalence... σ(m) good ⇒ nonempty. Fine. For m ≥ A. Also m+L ≥ A trivially. Fine.

Counting: each interval of L consecutive integers in [A,∞) contains exactly T terms: it contains each residue mod L once; membership depends only on residue? (4) says m term ⇔ m+L term, so membership periodic with period L on [A,∞). Interval [A, A+L-1] vs other intervals: shifting by L repeatedly covers any interval of length L contained in [A,∞). Yes, since any such interval [s, s+L-1] with s ≥ A can be pulled back: s = A + jL + r with 0 ≤ r < L... hmm, interval not necessarily aligned. Better argument: define f(m) = 1 if term, periodic mod L on [A,∞). For interval [s, s+L-1], the set of residues mod L is all residues. For each residue r mod L, need the indicator at residue r well-defined: values m ≥ A with m ≡ r mod L all give same answer — yes by repeated (4). So exactly T terms where T = count over any complete residue system ≥ A. [A, A+L-1] is a complete residue system mod L. Good.

(a_n, a_n + L]: contains exactly T terms. Terms are > a_n and ≤ a_n + L. Count: interval [a_n+1, a_n+L] length L, all ≥ A, contains T terms, and a_n+L is a term by (4) applied to m = a_n ≥ A. So the T terms are a_{n+1},...,a_{n+T}, and a_{n+T} ≤ a_n+L with a_{n+T} being the largest term ≤ a_n+L. Since a_n+L is a term and there are exactly T terms in the interval, a_{n+T} = a_n + L. Correct.

Also check pairwise non-coprimality: each new term shares factor with all previous, so gcd(a_{n+1}, a_i)>1 for i ≤ n, hence all pairs. Fine.

Unboundedness argument: M = least multiple of A greater than a_n; gcd(M, a_i) ≥ gcd(A,a_i) > 1. gcd(A,a_i)>1: A = a_1, a_i for i>1 shares factor with a_1. Yes. And M ≤ a_n + A. So sequence unbounded, also a_{n+1} exists (M admissible candidate), well-definedness of the greedy rule.

One edge: in the lemma, "choose p ∈ σ(x)" — need σ(x) nonempty, shown. Also case m = A: then m = R p^k = A, and σ(x) = P(A), which is good since P(A) good by (1). Fine.

Everything checks. Also σ(b) good ⇒ meets P(x): (2) uses goodness of σ(b) against term x. Good.

Also check hypothesis 3 counterexample irrelevant. Verdict: pass. Scores: correctness 4, completeness 4, rigor 4, self_contained 4.
